newsitem.title: AFGHANISTAN: Afghan Taleban defend recruiting Pakistani fighter.
newsitem.headline: Afghan Taleban defend recruiting Pakistani fighter.

text.p: A senior Taleban official on Friday defended the movement's recruitment of Pakistan nationals to fight in the war for control of Afghanistan.

Taleban Interior Minister Mullah Khairullah Khairkhwa's comments were in response to accusations levelled by Ahmed Shah Masood, the most important military commander in the administration ousted from Kabul last Septmeber.

"In response to the claims by Masood, there are a very limited number of Pakistani Taleban. They have no documents to prove any links with the Pakistan authorities; they are solely the people who have grown up and studied with Afghan Taleban," Khairkhwa told reporters in Kabul on Friday.
"The numbers are very limited, perhaps 1 in 100, I don't think that there are more than 50 in the whole of Afghanistan," he added.
The Taleban's opponents accuse the religious movement of being a creation of Pakistan, and say that there are large numbers of Pakistani nationals fighting in their ranks.

The opposition has said it captured at least 400 Pakistani prisoners when it retook the northern Afghan city of Mazar-i-Sharif from the Taleban at the end of May, but it has been impossible to independently verify the claim.
The Taleban say they are recruiting from the Pakistani madrassas -- Islamic colleges -- because most of the students there are of Afghan origin.
The United Nations estimates that there are still more than one million Afghans in Pakistan, most of them refugees from almost 20 years of continuous fighting in their homeland.
"Many of the students in Pakistan's madrassas are Afghan, therefore we recruit from the madrassas in Pakistan. We don't have any madrassas in Afghanistan," said Khairkhwa.

The Pakistan government has denied that it assists the Taleban or encourages its nationals to fight alongside them. The Afghan opposition says Pakistan authorities must be aware of the recruitment process.
"We cannot accept that the Pakistani authorities are completely unaware of this process," said opposition Foreign Minister Abdur Rahim Gaffurzai in a recent interview.
The name "Taleban" means religious student, and refers to the fact that many of the movement's initial recruits were from the Afghan diaspora studying in madrassas.

"We consider the taleban (religious students) to be the most sincere people. They are more willing to sacrifice their lives for the establishment of an Islamic state. That is why we recruit in Pakistan's madrassa," said Khairkhwa.

One Pakistan national fighting alongside the Taleban on the front line north of Kabul told reporters on Thursday that he had come to fight with the Taleban when his madrassa in Pakistan close to the Afghan border was shut. He said he arrived with 700 classmates.

"I was at a madrassa in Bannu that was affiliated with Fazlur Rahman (leader of the Pakistani politico-religious Jamiat-e-Ulema-e-Islam party). When Mazar fell they closed the madrassa and 700 of us came to fight with the Taleban," said the young man, who did not want to give his name.
He said that he would return to the madrassa when it reopened, although he did not know when that would be.

Khairkhwa said there were many Moslems who wanted to fight alongside the Taleban in their attempt to create a pure Islamic state in Afghanistan, and that the Taleban's Islamic principles prevented them from being turned away.
"This is the only place in the world where Sunni (Moslem) taleban and scholars are in power, therefore every Moslem in the world wants to contribute their share to increase that power.
"We follow Islamic principles, they do not allow us to prevent those who volunteer to fight Jihad (holy war) for the establishment of an Islamic state from taking part," said Khairkhwa.
